$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a bounded probability density supported on a compact
set $K\subset\mathbb R$. Let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure with a
continuous density bounded below by a positive constant on a neighborhood of
$K$. Assume
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered
normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ and
let $S\sim G$ be independent, where $G$ is any probability measure on
$(0,\infty)$. Suppose $n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$ for
$0<a_2<a_1<1$. Set $\sigma=\sigma_nS$ and
$$\delta_n:=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\ \sigma_n^2\log n\}.$$
Then, for some constant $C_1>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{(F,\sigma):\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le C_1\delta_n^2,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_{F,\sigma}}\right]^2\le C_1\delta_n^2\right\} \ge e^{-C_1n\delta_n^2}.$$
Here $p_{F,\sigma}$ is the density of [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]],
and all logarithmic integrands are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be supported on a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ with
$L<U$, let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ for a finite nonzero base measure whose
density is bounded below by a positive constant on a neighborhood of $I$, and let $S\sim G$ be
independent with $\sigma=\sigma_nS$. Put $R=(U-L)/2$ and, for $d>0$,
$I_d=[L-d,U+d]$.
Observe IID data from $p_0$ under the location-mixture density
$p_{F,\sigma}$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ with
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose the local KL
and log-square prior-mass condition gives a denominator event
$$P_0^n\{D_n\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}\}\longrightarrow1,$$
where $D_n=\int\prod_i p_{F,\sigma}(X_i)/p_0(X_i)\,\Pi_n(dF,d\sigma)$.
Choose $s_n\to0$ and put $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$, where $\Phi$ is the
standard normal distribution function. If
$$nq_n-(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2\to\infty,\qquad n\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0,$$
then the posterior complement of
$$\mathcal S_n:=\{(F,\sigma):\sigma\le s_n,\ F(I_d^c)\le\epsilon_n^2\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Fix $A\ge1$ independently of $n$. The constants in the entropy estimates
and the required fixed $M_0$ may depend on $A$. Let $0<a_2<a_1<1$,
$n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$, and
$\gamma>1$. Suppose $G$ is a probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ satisfying
$G((0,s])\le C e^{-\beta s^{-\gamma}}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$.
Let $s_n\to0$ with $s_n/\sigma_n\to\infty$. For integers $j$ with
$2^j\sigma_n\le s_n$, put $\widetilde r_n:=\min\{r_n,1/4\}$ and
$$\mathcal P_{n,j}:=\{p_{F,\sigma}:F([-A,A]^c)\le\widetilde r_n^2/8, \quad 2^j\sigma_n\le\sigma<2^{j+1}\sigma_n,\quad \sigma\le s_n\},$$
and let $\pi_{n,j}$ be the prior mass of the corresponding parameter band,
so $\pi_{n,j}\le G([2^j,2^{j+1}))$. Suppose $r_n>0$ and, for some fixed
sufficiently large $M_0$ (allowed to depend on $A$) and fixed
$\eta>\gamma/[2(\gamma-1)]$,
$$r_n\ge M_0\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n, n^{-1/2}\sigma_n^{-\eta}\}.$$
With $N_{n,j}=N(r_n,\mathcal P_{n,j},h)$, one has
$$e^{-nr_n^2}\sum_{j:2^j\sigma_n\le s_n}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0.$$
If instead $G$ is supported on a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, the same
conclusion holds under the first rate term alone.

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $\Pi_n$ be a prior on a measurable parameter
space $\Theta_n^*$, and let $p_\theta$ be a jointly measurable family of finite-valued densities
against one sigma-finite measure, and let $p_0$ be the true density for IID
data $X_1,\ldots,X_n$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ satisfy
$\delta_n\le\epsilon_n$, $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$, and
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose for a constant $C_0>0$ that
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\delta_n^2,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_\theta}\right]^2\le\delta_n^2\right\}\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}.$$
Let $S_n\subseteq\Theta_n^*$ be a measurable sieve with
$\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ in $P_0^n$-probability. Partition it into
countably many measurable sets $S_{n,j}$, put $\pi_{n,j}=\Pi_n(S_{n,j})$,
and let $N_{n,j}=N(\epsilon_n,\{p_\theta:\theta\in S_{n,j}\},h)$ be the
finite covering number as defined in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]], with centers in that density class, whenever $\pi_{n,j}>0$. If
$$e^{-n\epsilon_n^2}\sum_{j:\pi_{n,j}>0}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0,$$
then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$, the posterior mass of
$$\{\theta:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

derivations.claim: Put $d_n=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\sigma_n^2\log n\}$. By [F3], choose $C_1\ge1$ so the prior mass is at least $e^{-C_1nd_n^2}$ on a set where both local quantities are at most $C_1d_n^2$. Set $\bar d_n=\sqrt{C_1}d_n$. Then the mass is at least $e^{-n\bar d_n^2}$ and both quantities are at most $\bar d_n^2$. By [F4], except on an event of probability at most $(n\bar d_n^2)^{-1}$, the likelihood denominator is at least $e^{-3n\bar d_n^2}$. Also $n\bar d_n^2\ge C_1\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\to\infty$.

Choose a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$ in its interior and contained in the open interval where the density of $\alpha$ is continuous and strictly positive. Such an interval exists because the support is compact; its base density is bounded below on $I$. Put $R=(U-L)/2>0$ and $\kappa=\max\{a_1,1-4a_2,0\}<1$. The polynomial bandwidth bounds give $n\bar d_n^2\le Cn^\kappa(\log n)^2$. Choose $s_n=c_0(\log n)^{-1/2}$ with $c_0$ large enough that for some $\theta<1-\kappa$, $q_n:=2\Phi(-R/s_n)\ge n^{-\theta}$ eventually: integrating the standard normal density on $[R/s_n,R/s_n+1]$ gives the claimed lower bound once $R^2/(2c_0^2)<\theta$. Hence $nq_n-5n\bar d_n^2\to\infty$. Set $r_n=M_0\epsilon_n$ for a fixed sufficiently large $M_0$, and $\xi_n=\min\{r_n,1/4\}/\sqrt8$. We have $n\xi_n^2\to\infty$ and $\xi_n^{-2}\le Cn$: if $r_n<1/4$, use $\epsilon_n\ge n^{-1/2}\log n$ for all large $n$, and otherwise $\xi_n$ is fixed. Choose $d>0$ with $d^2/(2c_0^2)>4$ and $A\ge1$ large enough that $I_d=[L-d,U+d]\subseteq[-A,A]$. Then $n\xi_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0$. Applying [F5] gives posterior concentration on $\{F(I_d^c)\le\xi_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$. Since $[-A,A]^c\subseteq I_d^c$, the larger sieve $S_n=\{F([-A,A]^c)\le\xi_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$ also has $\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$.

Partition $S_n$ into dyadic scale bands $S_{n,j}=S_n\cap\{2^j\sigma_n\le\sigma<2^{j+1}\sigma_n\}$ for $2^j\sigma_n\le s_n$. Their prior masses are bounded by $G([2^j,2^{j+1}))$. Since $\xi_n^2=\min\{r_n,1/4\}^2/8$, [F6] applies at radius $r_n$ and gives $e^{-nr_n^2}\sum_j\sqrt{N(r_n,\{p_{F,\sigma}:(F,\sigma)\in S_{n,j}\},h) \,\Pi_n(S_{n,j})}\longrightarrow0.$ For compactly supported $G$, only finitely many bands have positive prior mass and the first rate term suffices.

If $G$ is compactly supported, put $\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\sigma_n^2\log n\}$, $r_n^{\mathrm c}=M_0\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ and $\xi_n^{\mathrm c}=\min\{r_n^{\mathrm c},1/4\}/\sqrt8$. Since $\sigma_n\to0$, $n(\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c})^2\ge\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\to\infty$ and $(\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c})^{-2}\le Cn$. Thus $n(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^2\to\infty$ and $(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^{-2}\le Cn$. Also $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$. Retain $I,s_n,d,A$ from step 1.2: its denominator, leakage bound, and exponential factor do not depend on the target radius, so the hypotheses of [F5] hold with $\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ and $\xi_n^{\mathrm c}$ in place of $\epsilon_n$ and $\xi_n$. It yields posterior sieve complement convergence for $S_n^{\mathrm c}=\{F([-A,A]^c)\le(\xi_n^{\mathrm c})^2,\sigma\le s_n\}$. The compact branch of [F6] supplies the weighted entropy condition at radius $r_n^{\mathrm c}$ using only the first rate term.

The prior is the measurable DP law from [F1], and [F2], [F8] give its jointly measurable density likelihoods. We have $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n$, so increasing $M_0$ if necessary ensures $\bar d_n\le r_n$; also $n\bar d_n^2,nr_n^2\to\infty$. Thus [F3] supplies the local prior-mass condition for [F7]. For general $G$, steps 1.2 and 1.3 provide a sieve with vanishing posterior complement and its weighted entropy condition. If $G$ is compactly supported, step 2.1 instead provides these two conditions at radius $r_n^{\mathrm c}$, and its bound $\bar d_n\le\sqrt{C_1}\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$ allows $M_0$ to be chosen so $\bar d_n\le r_n^{\mathrm c}$. Apply [F7] with local radius $\bar d_n$ and target radius $r_n$ in the general case, or $r_n^{\mathrm c}$ in the compact case. It follows that for every sufficiently large fixed $M_1$, the posterior outside $M_1M_0\epsilon_n$ (respectively $M_1M_0\epsilon_n^{\mathrm c}$) tends to zero in $P_0^n$-probability. Since $M_1M_0$ can be any sufficiently large fixed constant, this proves the stated rates. The measurability and dominated-likelihood requirements are supplied by [F1], [F2], and [F8], and [F9] fixes the conclusion's metric convention.

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a finite-valued probability density on $\mathbb R$
with compact support. Assume $p_0\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and, with the
integrands set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$,
$$\int_{\{p_0>0\}}\left[\left(\frac{p_0''}{p_0}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{p_0'}{p_0}\right)^4\right]p_0\,dx<\infty,$$
and assume there is $C<\infty$ such that
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$. Here $h$ is the root-L2 Hellinger
distance of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]], and
$\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation
$\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is a finite nonzero
measure with a continuous, strictly positive Lebesgue density on an open
interval containing $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$, and independently let

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: At every zero of the nonnegative differentiable function $p$, $p'=0$. At each accumulation point of its zero set, differentiation along zeros of $p'$ gives $p''=0$; isolated zeros form a countable set. Thus $p''=0$ almost everywhere on $\{p=0\}$. Put $r=p''/p$ on $\{p>0\}$ and zero elsewhere. Then $p''=rp$ almost everywhere, $\int r^2p=J$, and [F2] gives $\int|p''|\le\sqrt J$. Both $p$ and $p''$ are continuous and compactly supported.

Let $P_t f=f*\phi_{\sqrt t}$ for $t>0$. Direct differentiation of [F1] gives $\partial_t\phi_{\sqrt t}=\tfrac12\partial_x^2\phi_{\sqrt t}$. For fixed $x$ and $0<\varepsilon<t$, the differentiated integrand in $P_sp(x)$ is bounded on $s\in[\varepsilon,t]$ and the compact support of $p$ by $C_{x,\varepsilon,t}|p(z)|$; differentiation under the integral [F5] and two integrations by parts [F6] therefore give $\partial_sP_s p=\tfrac12P_s p''$. The boundary terms vanish because $p,p'$ have compact support. Dominated convergence [F9] makes $s\mapsto P_s p''(x)$ continuous on $[\varepsilon,t]$, so [F7] integrates the derivative there. Gaussian approximate identities converge uniformly on continuous compactly supported functions: split their convolution integral at $|z|\le\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the integrand difference, and its complement, whose normal mass tends to zero by scaling and integrability of [F1]. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ consequently yields $p-P_t p=-\tfrac12\int_0^tP_s p''\,ds$ pointwise; the omitted integral over $[0,\varepsilon]$ tends to zero because $|P_sp''(x)|\le\|p''\|_\infty$.

Fix $t>0$ and put $q=P_t p$. It is positive everywhere because $p$ is a nonzero nonnegative density and the Gaussian kernel is positive; Tonelli [F3] and $\int\phi_{\sqrt t}=1$ show $q$ integrates to one. For $0<s\le t$, the Gaussian formula gives $\phi_{\sqrt t}(z)\ge\sqrt{s/t}\,\phi_{\sqrt s}(z)$ for every $z$, hence $q\ge\sqrt{s/t}P_s p$. Applying [F2] inside the convolution and then [F3] gives $|P_s p''|^2\le(P_s p)P_s(r^2p)$ and therefore $\int |P_s p''|^2/q\le\sqrt{t/s}\int P_s(r^2p)=\sqrt{t/s}J$. These inequalities remain valid if one of the pointwise nonnegative integrals is infinite.

Apply [F2] to the time integral in step 2.1 with weights $w(s)=(t/s)^{1/4}$. Since $\int_0^t w(s)ds=4t/3$, it gives $|p-q|^2\le\tfrac14(4t/3)\int_0^t w(s)^{-1}|P_s p''|^2ds$. Divide by $q$, integrate and use [F3] and step 2.2. The result is $\int(p-q)^2/q\le\tfrac14(4t/3)J\int_0^t(t/s)^{1/4}ds=(4/9)t^2J$. In particular all these weighted integrals are finite.

For $u>0$, the function $u-1-\log u$ has value zero at $1$ and derivative $(u-1)/u$, so $\log u\le u-1$ and $u\log u-u+1\le(u-1)^2$. For $t\ge1$, $t-t^{-1}-2\log t$ has value zero at $1$ and derivative $(t-1)^2/t^2\ge0$; replacing $t$ by $1/t$ gives $2|\log t|\le|t-t^{-1}|$ also for $0<t<1$. With $u=t^2$, this yields $u(\log u)^2\le(u-1)^2$. At $u=0$, use the conventions $u\log u=u(\log u)^2=0$, for which both inequalities hold. Apply these pointwise bounds to $u=p/q$ and integrate against $q$. Since $p,q$ integrate to one, [F4] identifies the first integral as KL; its negative part is integrable because $u\log u\ge-e^{-1}$. Both requested logarithmic quantities are at most the chi-square integral from step 3.1. Taking $t=\sigma^2$ proves the Statement.

Assume AC. Let $p\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be a nonnegative compactly supported probability density and suppose
$$J:=\int_{\{p>0\}}\frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)}\,dx<\infty.$$
For $\sigma>0$, set $q_\sigma=p*\phi_\sigma$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Then
$$\int\frac{(p-q_\sigma)^2}{q_\sigma}\,dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_\sigma)\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \int p\left[\log\frac p{q_\sigma}\right]^2dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J.$$
The logarithmic integrands are zero where $p=0$. No unimodality or uniform bound on $p/q_\sigma$ is assumed.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad \|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

Assume AC, let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure of total mass $m$, and
let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$. Consider a finite partition
$(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ with $\alpha(U_0)=0$ or
$0<\alpha(U_0)\le m$. Write $\alpha_j=\alpha(U_j)$ for $j\ge1$, and assume
$$a\eta^b\le\alpha_j\le1\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad 0<\eta<1/4,\qquad N\eta\le1/4,$$
for fixed $a,b>0$. For every $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_N)$ in the probability
simplex, there are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$
such that
$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad \min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$
For any compact $J\subset(0,m]$, the constants may instead depend only on
$a,b,m,J$ and are uniform over $\alpha(U_0)\in J$.
When $\alpha(U_0)=0$, the zero-base cell has $F(U_0)=0$ almost surely and is
omitted from the Dirichlet vector.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$, possible because these compact intervals exhaust $(0,\infty)$. Set $b_n=\sigma_n$, $\tau=s_-b_n$, $B=a+6$ and $\eta=b_n^B$. For all large $n$, partition each nondegenerate component of $K$ into equal consecutive Borel intervals of lengths in $[\tau/8,\tau/4]$: use $\lceil4\ell/\tau\rceil$ pieces for a component of length $\ell$. Endpoints can be assigned arbitrarily because $P_0$ has a density. The support of a continuous density has no isolated points, so there are no isolated support components to treat. There are $O(b_n^{-1})$ coarse cells $I_k$, each of mass at least $c' b_n^a$. Translate the conditional probability $P_0(\cdot\mid I_k)$ to an interval centered at zero, apply [F2] at scale $\tau$, and translate back. Multiplying by $P_0(I_k)$ and summing gives a finite probability $F_n$ with at most $C b_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$ atoms in the closures of these cells, each carrying its original coarse-cell label, and $\|p_{F_n,\tau}-p_{P_0,\tau}\|_\infty\le\eta/\tau$. The total weight of atoms with label $k$ is exactly $P_0(I_k)$.

Put $\delta=\eta\tau$. Move each atom to a nearest point of the global lattice of mesh $\delta$ and merge atoms at the same location. Preserve its fractional label weights when merging. The resulting distinct locations $z_j$ are separated by at least $\delta$, with weights $w_j$ summing to one, and still number $N\le Cb_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$. Let $U_j=[z_j-\delta/4,z_j+\delta/4)$ and $U_0=\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^NU_j$. These are disjoint partition cells. The base density is bounded above and below on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so $c_0\eta\tau\le\alpha(U_j)\le C_0\eta\tau\le1$ eventually. Since $B>1$, $\eta\tau\ge c_1\eta^2$ and $N\eta\to0$. Also $\sum_j\alpha(U_j)\le C N\delta\to0$, so, writing $m=\alpha(\mathbb R)>0$, we have $\alpha(U_0)\in[m/2,m]$ eventually.

Apply [F3] with tolerance $\eta$ to get an event $E_n$ on which $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta$ and $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Its constants can be taken uniform in $n$: in the proof of [F3] the only residual-parameter factors are $\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ and a lower bound $(\eta^2/2)^m$ for the residual power. The gamma ratio is bounded below on the fixed compact interval $[m/2,m]$, and the latter power already has fixed exponent $m$. The remaining constants use only the fixed bound $c_1\eta^2\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Finally $\log(e/\eta)\le C\log n$ by the polynomial lower bandwidth bound.

For $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, the original discrete approximation still satisfies $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$. Indeed the Gaussian convolution identity $\phi_u*\phi_v=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}$ follows by completing the square and integrating; convolution with a probability kernel contracts the supremum norm by the triangle inequality. Use $u=\tau$, $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\tau^2}$, treating equality by the original approximation. Differentiating [F5] gives $\|\phi_\sigma'\|_\infty\le C\sigma^{-2}$. Atom relocation by at most $\delta/2$ therefore changes the mixture by at most $C\delta/\sigma^2\le C\eta/b_n$. For $F\in E_n$, replacing each $F|_{U_j}$ by its mass at $z_j$ costs at most the same derivative bound times $\delta/4$; the weight discrepancies and residual mass cost at most $3\eta\|\phi_\sigma\|_\infty$. Consequently, uniformly over $F\in E_n$ and $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, one has $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$.

For any $x\in K$ choose a coarse cell whose closure contains $x$. Its length is at most $\tau/4$, so every original atom with that label, and every associated relocated atom-cell, lies in $[x-\tau,x+\tau]$ eventually. Let $J_x$ be the set of relocated atom indices carrying a positive fraction of this label's weight. Merging preserves the full label weight, so $\sum_{j\in J_x}w_j\ge P_0(I_k)\ge c' b_n^a$. The vector discrepancy on $E_n$ implies $F([x-\tau,x+\tau])\ge\sum_{j\in J_x}F(U_j)\ge c'b_n^a-3\eta\ge c'b_n^a/2$. On this neighborhood, [F5] is at least $c''/b_n$ for every $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$. Thus $p_{F,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$. The same argument directly with the coarse-cell mass under $P_0$ gives $p_{P_0,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$, after decreasing the constant.

Put $q=p_{P_0,\sigma}$ and $r=p_{F,\sigma}$. The mean-value theorem for the logarithm, whose derivative is given by [F6], and steps 4.1, 4.2 give $\sup_{x\in K}|\log(q(x)/r(x))|\le C\eta b_n^{-a}=Cb_n^6$. By [F1], $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert Q)\le Cb_n^4$ and $P_0[\log(p_0/q)]^2\le Cb_n^4$ uniformly in these scales. Adding the bounded log perturbation proves $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le Cb_n^4+Cb_n^6\le C'b_n^4$. The inequality $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$ similarly gives $P_0[\log(p_0/r)]^2\le C'b_n^4$. All integrals exist by the displayed bounds, and integrands vanish off $\{p_0>0\}$.

The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has fixed probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. Therefore $E_n$ times this event is contained in the displayed KL/log-square set and has probability at least $g\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Increase $C_2$ to absorb $g$. Since $nd_n^2\ge b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2$ and $d_n^2\ge b_n^4$, the consequent local-radius form follows as well. This proves all assertions without a unimodality hypothesis.
